AbstractOverviewData collectionResultsCitation
01 · Motivation

Abstract

Dexterous ManipulationBenchmark

Long-horizon dexterous manipulation remains a fundamental challenge for robot learning, requiring the composition of multiple skills, precise bimanual coordination, generalizable visual understanding, and robust skill transitions. Yet existing manipulation benchmarks largely emphasize isolated skills or support only a limited range of end-effectors, making these capabilities difficult to evaluate systematically. We introduce DexArena, a benchmark designed to evaluate learning and generalization in long-horizon bimanual dexterous manipulation. DexArena features 10 long-horizon tasks and 30 stage-level tasks spanning diverse household and industrial scenarios. Each long-horizon task is composed of explicitly defined stages with physically grounded success conditions, enabling reliable evaluation of both intermediate progress and end-to-end task completion. A unified benchmark interface and verified human-teleoperated demonstrations enable testing different policy learning algorithms, with standardized simulation configurations, scene randomization, trajectory replay, and task-level evaluation. Through extensive baseline experiments, we identify substantial challenges in precise manipulation, generalization to scene variation, and skill composition. DexArena establishes a challenging and reproducible benchmark for developing robot learning methods that move toward generalizable long-horizon dexterous behavior.

Primary area: applications to robotics, autonomy, planning.

02 · Benchmark design

Skills and sequences in a shared physical setting.

Ten complete tasks and thirty matched stage environments connect household, laboratory and industrial interactions. Persistent physical predicates measure both intermediate progress and complete behavior.

03 · Demonstrations

From human motion to replayable demonstrations.

VR wrist tracking and glove inputs are mapped into absolute arm and hand targets. Episodes then pass through review, export and replay validation, with recorded simulator states retained for offline multi-view rendering.

Replay-successful demonstrations

100 episodes per canonical stage, recorded at 20 Hz.

Embodiment

29 dimensions with one hand. 58 with two.

The released canonical data uses Panda arms with 22-DoF Sharpa hands and absolute joint-position targets: 7 arm + 22 hand joints per side.

  • Single-arm and bimanual variants
  • Shared task and success interfaces
  • Parallel-jaw, Sharpa, Wuji, and XHand simulation support

Experimental results

Learning a skill is only the beginning.

Six baselines evaluated on execution, visual generalization and long-horizon composition. All scores below are reported in the supplied manuscript.

01 / 30 stages · training scene

Strong individual skills.

GR00T records the highest average success in the training scene. ACT and RLPD follow, but no method consistently solves every stage.

+3.4 ppadvantage over ACT
Stage-level results ↗
02 / 30 stages × 3 native scenes

A different scene changes the ranking.

π0.5 leads across three held-out kitchens. Its average is 2.9 percentage points below the training-scene result; the same policy is evaluated without adaptation.

+3.8 ppadvantage over ACT
Cross-scene results ↗
03 / 10 sequences · no stage resets

The sequence remains the challenge.

π0.5 and ACT report non-zero average success on complete sequences. Successful individual stages do not yet translate into reliable end-to-end behavior.

2 / 6methods with non-zero sequence success
